newsitem.title: JAPAN: Shareholder sues Sumitomo over copper loss fund.
newsitem.headline: Shareholder sues Sumitomo over copper loss fund.

text.p: A Sumitomo Corp. shareholder Thursday sued the Japanese trading house to try to block it from setting up a special fund to pay for the massive losses in copper trading disclosed earlier this year.

Sumitomo jumped back into the headlines last week when, after months of silence on the copper scandal, it announced that it had raised its estimate of the copper trading losses to $2.6 billion from the $1.8 billion it announced on June 13.

The company's shareholder meeting was held on June 27, just two weeks after Sumitomo announced huge losses from unauthorised copper trades over a 10-year period. The suit contends that the vote to set up the fund and cancel a share buyback scheme was taken improperly.

Several of those who attended the meeting have complained they were shunted into side rooms to watch the proceedings on television, with no chance to question executives, while the main room was filled with Sumitomo employees.

The shareholders' meeting lasted less than 40 minutes. It approved by voice vote, with no casting of ballots, the company's plans to cover the massive copper losses by setting up a separate fund and cancelling a share buy-back.

"I thought it was strange that the shareholders' meeting ended without any objections, despite the occurrence of such a major incident," Kazuyoshi Yuoka, who filed the suit, said in a telephone interview.
Yuoka said he had been sitting in the main room where the meeting was being held.

"I was so frustrated with Sumitomo's undemocratic way of conducting the shareholders' meeting. Although I raised my hand, the Sumitomo side did not allow me to ask detailed questions on copper trading losses," he said.
"The shareholders' meeting was well prepared and just a ceremony for the Sumitomo management."
A team of lawyers is helping Yuoka in the lawsuit.

"Yuoka is not necessarily opposed to the special fund, but is opposed to the fact that it was neither discussed nor debated," one of the lawyers said. "He is also opposed to the fact that the company did not reveal the extent of the retirement payments."

A Sumitomo spokesman said the suit, filed in district court in Osaka, the western Japanese city where Sumitomo is based, sought to repeal approval of the fund and of retirement payments to five members of the board of directors.

"If this case is requesting the repeal of resolutions at our general shareholders' meeting, it is our belief that the meeting was held for the shareholders themselves and that procedurally it was in accord with commercial law, and therefore there are no problems with it," Sumitomo said in a statement.
It has blamed the losses on unauthorised trades over 10 years by its former copper trader, Yasuo Hamanaka.
When Sumitomo disclosed the higher estimated loss on Friday, it also accused Hamanaka of forgery and breach of trust and said it planned to press charges against him.
The company fired Hamanaka on June 14, the day after the losses were first disclosed and has not said if the former star trader was cooperating with its internal investigation.
Hamanaka has remained largely in seclusion since the affair broke.
